passages.t: The tabernacle and the Day of Atonement
passages.happening:
“Now the first covenant had regulations for worship and also an earthly sanctuary” (verse 1).

The writer describes the tabernacle. In its first room, the Holy Place, were the lampstand, the table and the consecrated bread. “Behind the second curtain was a room called the Most Holy Place” (verse 3), with the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant. Inside the ark were the jar of manna, Aaron's staff that had budded, and the stone tablets. Above it were “the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the mercy seat. But we cannot discuss these things in detail now” (verse 5).

The priests went into the first room regularly. “But only the high priest entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance” (verse 7).

“By this arrangement the Holy Spirit was showing that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing. It is an illustration for the present time, because the gifts and sacrifices being offered were unable to cleanse the conscience of the worshiper” (verses 8-9). They were “external regulations imposed until the time of reform” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The tabernacle was the tent Israel carried in the wilderness, where God lived among his people. It had two rooms. In the outer room, the Holy Place, stood a lampstand, a table with twelve loaves of bread, renewed every Sabbath, and the altar where incense was burned. A thick curtain hung before the inner room, the Most Holy Place. There stood the ark of the covenant, a chest covered in gold, holding the stone tablets of the law. Over its lid, called the mercy seat, two golden cherubim spread their wings. The writer describes the tent of the wilderness, not the later temple, because he is reading Scripture.

On one day each year, the Day of Atonement, the high priest went behind the curtain. He took blood, first for his own sins and then for the people's, and sprinkled it on and before the mercy seat. A second goat, the scapegoat, was sent out into the wilderness, carrying the people's sins away.

The writer sees a lesson in the shape of the tent itself. Only one man, once a year, could go into God's presence. The curtain said, ‘not yet’. The way to God was real, but it was not yet open to all.

‘Unable to cleanse the conscience.’ The conscience is the inner sense of guilt. The writer says the sacrifices dealt with outward cleanness, ‘food and drink and special washings’, but could not by themselves make the inner person clean before God. They were given ‘until the time of reform’, the time when God would set things right.
passages.ot:
The building of the tabernacle fills the end of Exodus. God told Moses where the curtain should hang: “So the veil will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place” (Exodus 26:33).

The Day of Atonement is in Leviticus 16. Aaron could not go behind the veil whenever he chose (Leviticus 16:2). He offered a bull for himself, then a goat for the people. Then he laid his hands on a second goat “and confess over it all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites” (Leviticus 16:21), and it was sent into the wilderness. The purpose of the day was given in God's own words: “because on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, and you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD” (Leviticus 16:30).

And God promised real forgiveness through the sacrifices: “in this way the priest will make atonement on their behalf, and they will be forgiven” (Leviticus 4:20). The psalms sing of it: “As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12).
passages.hard:
If God promised forgiveness through the sacrifices (Leviticus 4:20), how can Hebrews say they could not cleanse the conscience? Was Israel's worship empty?

No. God gave the tabernacle and its sacrifices, and Israelites who came to him in faith were truly forgiven, as Leviticus promises and the psalms celebrate. Hebrews does not deny that. It says something about where that forgiveness came from. Later in this chapter it says that Christ's death redeemed people ‘from the transgressions committed under the first covenant’ (verse 15). Many Christians read this as meaning that the faithful of Israel were forgiven on the ground of the sacrifice still to come, as Paul speaks of God passing over sins committed beforehand (Romans 3:25). The animal sacrifices were God's own way of pointing to it, and of teaching his people that sin is costly and that God himself provides the way back.

So Hebrews is not mocking Israel's worship. It is reading its shape as a sign, given by the Holy Spirit, of something still to come. For centuries some Christians used this letter, with other parts of the New Testament, to teach contempt for Jews and Judaism. That reading is false. This site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why.

A smaller puzzle: Exodus places the golden incense altar in front of the curtain, in the outer room (Exodus 30:6), but verse 4 lists it with the inner room. Some think the Greek word means the golden censer the high priest carried into the inner room. Others note that the Old Testament links the incense altar closely with the inner room, so the writer may mean what belonged to it in use. He himself says he is not giving a detailed account (verse 5).
passages.asks: The curtain said ‘not yet’. Ask what it would have meant to stand outside it all your life, and what it means that the way in is now open. Ask whether your conscience has been cleansed, or only your outside tidied. And ask whether you honour the patient way God taught his people over many centuries.

passages.t: Christ's own blood, and a clean conscience
passages.happening:
“But when Christ came as high priest of the good things that have come, He went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands and is not a part of this creation. He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption” (verses 11-12).

“For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean sanctify them so that their bodies are clean, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!” (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
‘But when Christ came’ is the turn of the chapter. Everything in verses 1 to 10 is now answered.

The high priest went into a tent made by human hands. Christ went into the true sanctuary, God's own presence. The high priest took the blood of animals. Christ gave his own life. The high priest went in every year. Christ went in ‘once for all’. The high priest's work had to be repeated. Christ secured ‘eternal redemption’, a release that lasts forever. ‘Redemption’ means setting a captive or a slave free by paying a price.

‘By His own blood’ does not mean Christ carried blood into heaven like the high priest carried it into the tent. Most readers take it to mean that his death, his life given, is what opened the way for him and for us.

The ‘ashes of a heifer’ were mixed with water to cleanse people who had touched a dead body, so that they could worship again. That was a cleanness of the body. The writer argues from the lesser to the greater: if that was real, how much more the blood of Christ, which cleanses the conscience.

‘Through the eternal Spirit’: most take this as the Holy Spirit, by whom Christ offered himself; some take it as Christ's own divine spirit. On the first reading, here in one verse are the Son, the Spirit and the Father: Christ offered himself through the eternal Spirit to God.

‘Works of death’ may mean sins that lead to death, or deeds done in a dead way. Either way, the cleansed conscience is set free ‘to serve the living God’.
passages.ot:
The red heifer is in Numbers 19. Its ashes were kept “for preparing the water of purification; this is for purification from sin” (Numbers 19:9), used for anyone who had touched a corpse.

‘Unblemished’ is the word the law used for sacrificial animals, which had to be without defect. Christ offered himself without any blemish of sin.

The longing for a clean heart, not only clean hands, runs through the psalms: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10). The same psalm says, “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (Psalm 51:17). The prophets, too, warned that sacrifices without a changed heart meant nothing to God (Isaiah 1:11; Micah 6:6-8).
passages.asks: Christ cleanses the conscience. Ask what still weighs on your conscience, and whether you have brought it to him or keep carrying it yourself. Ask whether you are trying to clean yourself with ‘works of death’. And ask what it would mean, set free, to ‘serve the living God’ today.

passages.t: The new covenant comes into force through a death
passages.happening:
“Therefore Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, now that He has died to redeem them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant” (verse 15).

“In the case of a will, it is necessary to establish the death of the one who made it, because a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died” (verses 16-17).

“That is why even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood” (verse 18). Moses read every commandment to the people, then took blood, with water, scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled the scroll and the people, “saying, ‘This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep.’” (verse 20). He sprinkled the tabernacle and its vessels too.

“According to the law, in fact, nearly everything must be purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Verse 15 says that Christ's death reaches backward as well as forward. It redeems ‘from the transgressions committed under the first covenant’. The faithful of Israel, who looked to God through the sacrifices he gave, are included in what Christ did.

Then a play on words. The Greek word for ‘covenant’ was also the everyday word for a ‘will’, the paper that says who receives what when someone dies. The writer uses that second meaning for a moment. A will takes effect only when the one who made it has died. In the same way, the new covenant, with its promised ‘inheritance’, comes into force through Christ's death. His death was not an accident that stopped his work. It was the act that put the covenant into effect.

Then he goes back to Sinai. Even the first covenant began with blood. Moses sprinkled the blood of sacrifices on the people and said, ‘This is the blood of the covenant.’ Blood stood for life given up in death. A covenant sealed with blood was solemn: life was at stake.

‘Nearly everything’ is careful. The law allowed a poor person to bring flour instead of an animal for a sin offering, and some things were cleansed with water or fire. But blood was at the centre.
passages.ot:
The covenant ceremony at Sinai is in Exodus 24. The people said, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient” (Exodus 24:7). “So Moses took the blood, sprinkled it on the people, and said, ‘This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.’” (Exodus 24:8). Hebrews adds the water, scarlet wool and hyssop, which appear in other cleansing rites of the law (such as Leviticus 14 and Numbers 19).

The meaning of blood is given in Leviticus: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar” (Leviticus 17:11). Notice ‘I have given it to you’. The sacrifice was God's gift to his people, not a bribe from them to him.

The exception for the poor is in Leviticus 5: “if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two young pigeons, he may bring a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a sin offering” (Leviticus 5:11).
passages.hard:
‘Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.’ Why blood? Does God need death before he will forgive?

Start with Leviticus 17:11. Blood stands for life, and God says, ‘I have given it to you’. In Israel the sacrifice was God's own provision, given in mercy, so that sinners could live. It was never a way of buying off an angry god. Abraham's words on the mountain point the same way: “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son” (Genesis 22:8).

Hebrews says that what the animal sacrifices pictured, Christ fulfilled. Sin is not a small thing. It breaks the covenant and brings death. Forgiveness is free to us, but it is not cheap. In Christ, God himself bore the cost.

Christians describe how the cross saves in several ways, and the doctrine study ‘Sacrifice and Atonement’ sets them out. Many hold that Christ bore the judgment sin deserves in the place of sinners, and they stress that this is not an angry Father punishing an unwilling Son, but the triune God, in love, taking the cost into himself. Others stress the cross as God's victory over sin, death and the devil, as Hebrews 2:14-15 does, or as the great showing of God's love. Many hold that these belong together. These notes do not choose between the ways of saying it.

What about verses 16 and 17? Some readers prefer to translate the word as ‘covenant’ throughout: a covenant sealed with a death, the death the covenant's curse demands, borne by Christ. Most English Bibles, including the Berean Standard Bible, read ‘will’ here. On either reading, the point is the same: the new covenant comes into force through Christ's death.
passages.asks: The covenant was sealed with blood, and God himself provided the sacrifice. Ask what it means that your forgiveness cost something, and who paid it. Ask whether you treat forgiveness as cheap. And ask what ‘inheritance’ you have been called to receive.

passages.t: Once for all, and a second appearing
passages.happening:
“So it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God” (verses 23-24).

He did not enter to offer himself again and again, as the high priest went in every year. “Otherwise, Christ would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But now He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself” (verse 26).

“Just as man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment, so also Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many; and He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him” (verses 27-28).
passages.hearers:
‘The heavenly things themselves’ needing purifying is one of the puzzles of the letter. Some readers think of heaven opened to sinners, the whole way of coming to God made clean. Others think of God's people themselves, whose consciences are cleansed. The writer does not explain. His point is that Christ's sacrifice is greater because what it does is greater.

‘To appear on our behalf in the presence of God.’ The high priest went in hidden by a cloud of incense, so that he would not see God's glory and die. Christ appears openly before God's face, for us.

‘Once for all’ comes again and again in these chapters. If Christ's sacrifice were like the old ones, he would have had to suffer over and over through all of history. But he suffered once, ‘at the end of the ages’, the time of fulfilment, and that was enough.

Then a comparison. Every person dies once, and then faces God's judgment. Christ, too, died once, ‘to bear the sins of many’. And he will come back, ‘a second time’. When he comes, it will not be to deal with sin again; that was finished. It will be ‘to bring salvation’ to those waiting for him.
passages.ot:
‘To bear the sins of many’ comes from Isaiah's song of the servant of the LORD: “Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12).

The Old Testament speaks of a judgment where nothing is hidden: “For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil” (Ecclesiastes 12:14).

And on the Day of Atonement the high priest went in with incense, and “the cloud of incense will cover the mercy seat above the Testimony, so that he will not die” (Leviticus 16:13).
passages.hard:
‘Man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment’ (verse 27). What does this verse say, and what does it not say?

It says that every human life is lived once, and that each person will answer to God. Many readers note that it leaves no room for ideas of living many lives over again. And its main purpose is a comparison: as a human dies once, so Christ was offered once. His death does not need repeating, any more than ours will be.

It does not tell us when the judgment comes, or what happens between a person's death and that day. Christians differ on some details of that time, as the doctrine study ‘Death and the Intermediate State’ sets out, but all confess that those who belong to Christ are his in death and will rise. And the verse does not say how God will judge any particular person. That belongs to God alone.

What it does say about believers is full of hope. The one who will come is the one who bore their sins. He comes ‘to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him’.

If you are grieving someone who has died, these verses do not ask you to stop grieving. Jesus wept at his friend's grave (John 11:35). Paul says believers grieve, but not “like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Christ will appear a second time. Ask whether you are among ‘those who eagerly await Him’, or whether his coming feels far off or frightening. Ask what it means that the judge is the one who bore your sins. And ask how living once, and only once, should shape what you do with today.
